newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Ethics to guide Swiss on Holocaust accounts - Berne.
newsitem.headline: Ethics to guide Swiss on Holocaust accounts - Berne.

text.p: Switzerland will consider ethics as well as the letter of the law when deciding what to do with any unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims it finds and for which no heirs have emerged, the foreign ministry said on Friday.

"We won't be protecting ourselves only behind legal parameters. There is the law and there is ethics. We will make a due mixture of the two things," ministry spokesman Jean-Philippe Tissieres said, but he added he could not be more precise.

He recalled that Switzerland gave the local Jewish community and a Zurich refugee aid group nearly 10 million Swiss francs ($8 million) it found during a sweep of dormant bank accounts ordered in 1962 to find the lost wealth of victims of Nazi oppression.
"This ethical principle had already been applied in the past and there is no reason at all not to apply the same kind of principle (again)," he told Reuters.

Switzerland has faced a barrage of criticism from Jewish groups and a U.S. senator who charge it has not done enough to turn up unclaimed wealth of Jews who hid their wealth here before perishing at the hands of Hitler's Nazis.
Holocaust survivors have filed two class-action lawsuits in U.S. courts seeking a full accounting of the funds' fate.

Switzerland has struggled to respond to headlines, fuelled by documents from archives, showing the Swiss agreed to give Poland and Hungary their citizens' unclaimed wealth as part of post-war accords compensating Swiss for nationalised property.

But it is slowly finding its feet, pointing out many of the "secret" deals had actually been openly discussed at the time and simply reflected international private law that says heirless assets belong to the state where the owner last lived.

The Neue Zuercher Zeitung newspaper, a bastion of the conservative Swiss establishment, on Friday reprinted part of its report from 1950 showing the Swiss president at the time, Max Petitpierre, outlined the 1949 Polish accord to parliament.
Critics have assailed the agreement to hand over missing Poles' dormant accounts to Warsaw, but Petitpierre said the accord safeguarded any owners that might eventually be found.

"The rights of the owners and their heirs are fully preserved," he was quoted as saying, pointing out the treaty called for Poland to reimburse Swiss banks or insurance companies for future claims on any assets they had transferred.

Switzerland also struck post-war compensation accords with Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Romania. It is still checking whether they contained similar provisions on unclaimed assets and whether any money ever changed hands.

Swiss banks have never disputed they were a popular refuge for the wealth of European Jews fearing Nazi persecution after Hitler came to power in Germany in 1933. Many were drawn by Switzerland's strict bank secrecy and neutral status.
But the banks reject Jewish groups' claims that they may be sitting on billions of dollars in assets left behind by Jewish account holders murdered in the Holocaust.
Officials say they are doing their best to check allegations about lost Holocaust wealth that are drawing worldwide attention and hurting Switzerland's reputation as a financial centre.

A banking ombudsman is helping nearly 1,000 claimants track down any lost accounts that may have escaped two previous sweeps of their records. A separate panel agreed by Swiss bankers and Jewish groups is also set to comb banks' records.

Parliament is set to give final approval in December to a group of experts empowered to lift banking secrecy and probe Switzerland's wartime commerce with the Nazis, including big gold purchases that helped finance the German war effort.
